newsitem.title: USA: Former mayor weighing rematch in NYC race.
newsitem.headline: Former mayor weighing rematch in NYC race.

text.p: Former Mayor David Dinkins said Thursday he was seriously weighing an election rematch with Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, a move that would liven up an otherwise lackluster race led by the Republican incumbent.
Political observers warned, however, that Dinkins, who narrowly lost to Giuliani three years ago, would have a tough time beating the heavily favoured mayor.
Dinkins told a news conference that several friends have urged him to run again for the job he lost in 1993.
"I said I'll think about it. I'll consider it," he said.

Opinion polls show Giuliani with a substantial lead over the four Democrats mounting official challenges so far -- Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger, Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer, activist minister Rev. Al Sharpton and Brooklyn Councilman Sal Albanese.
Those polls indicate a majority of New Yorkers are satisfied with the quality of life in the city, which is enjoying the lowest crime rate in a generation.
That voter satisfaction is one reason political columnist Michael Tomasky of New York magazine called the idea of a Dinkins' candidacy "pretty cockeyed."

"I don't hear very many people pining for the glory days of the Dinkins administration," Tomasky said. "It assumes that Giuliani hasn't expanded his base or his vote-getting potential, which it seems to me he certainly has."
Asked at City Hall about Dinkins' possible entry into the race, Giuliani said simply, "I would welcome his candidacy."
Lee Meringhoff, a pollster at the Marist Institute in Poughkeepsie, New York, called Dinkins "a long shot."
"He needs to establish a rationale beyond it being just a rematch or what might look like just a grudge match," he said.

Dinkins was the city's first black mayor, defeating Mayor Ed Koch in the 1989 Democratic primary and Giuliani in the 1989 general election. But Giuliani, a former federal prosecutor, came back to beat Dinkins four years later.
Dinkins insisted Giuliani is "beatable" by either of the two borough presidents or by himself. He criticised the mayor for tolerating abusive police tactics, especially against minorities.
"This administration is dangerously close to having adopted a philosophy that the end justifies the means," he said.
Since leaving City Hall, Dinkins has been hosting a radio show and teaching urban policy at Columbia University.
His flirtation with City Hall helps illustrate the weak position of the other Democrats, most of whom are not well-known beyond their narrow political constituencies, analysts said.
"A lot of people don't think Ruth (Messinger) or Freddie (Ferrer) can win, so they're casting about for someone who can," Tomasky said. "But they hooked the wrong fish."
Dinkins argued that the mayor has weak support among voters on issues of education, the budget and welfare. And he called him a "bully" who "rules through fear and intimidation."
Dinkins admitted he has not formed an exploratory campaign committee nor discussed the idea extensively with his family.

Asked about Dinkins' possible run, Messinger told local television: "David Dinkins has suggested over several years that he's been there and done that.... I expect to win the primary and defeat the mayor in November."
Ferrer said he would respect Dinkins' decision, saying he "owes it to himself to think about a re-entry into public service."
Albanese said he thought Dinkins would decide not to run. Sharpton said he thought the issue demonstrated the inability of Democrats to solidify support behind one candidate.
